summary: This informational memo gives a taxonomy of architectures in existing IEEE 802.11 products. It analyses wireless LAN functions and describes how they are split between entities such as access points and controllers.

eli5.summary: Wi-fi systems divide jobs between access points and a central controller in different ways. This document sorts them into types.

subtitle: Classification of wireless access point network designs

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.11 wireless networks can be implemented in many different ways by vendors, but there is no standardized taxonomy to understand and compare these different architectural approaches.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes 16 vendor submissions and classifies WLAN access network architectures into three main families based on how IEEE 802.11 functions are distributed: Autonomous (all in one device), Centralized (functions split between access points and a central controller), and Distributed Mesh (peer-to-peer).
tldr.outcome: The taxonomy provides common terminology and understanding of existing WLAN architectures, supporting standards development and vendor interoperability efforts by identifying where standards need to define interfaces between architectural components.

today: RFC 4118 is an Informational document that remains the authoritative taxonomy of WLAN access network architectures. It has not been obsoleted and continues to serve as a reference for understanding different approaches to access point control and provisioning. The CAPWAP working group later developed protocols to standardize the control channel between WTPs and ACs across these architectural families.

sections.title: The Need for WLAN Architecture Classification
sections.content:
As IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN (WLAN) technology matured and networks scaled from small deployments to enterprise-wide systems, vendors faced new challenges in managing, monitoring, and controlling large numbers of access points. Distributing and maintaining consistent configuration across many devices proved difficult, and the shared wireless medium required effective coordination to minimize interference and maximize performance.

Vendors responded with diverse solutions, some proprietary and some based on similar principles, but without a common framework. This RFC provides the first taxonomy of WLAN architectures by analyzing products from 15 WLAN vendors and one academic research group. By classifying existing approaches, the document establishes common terminology and enables standardization of the interfaces between architectural components.
sections.eli5: Managing many Wi-Fi access points is hard. Different companies built different solutions, so nobody could compare them or mix equipment from different vendors. This document organizes the solutions into categories.

sections.title: IEEE 802.11 Functions and CAPWAP Functions
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11 defines 802.11 Functions required by the wireless standard, including station services (authentication, de-authentication, MSDU delivery, confidentiality) and distribution system services (association, disassociation, reassociation, distribution, integration). Additional required services include beacon generation, probe response, frame processing, synchronization, retransmission, rate adaptation, and privacy.

CAPWAP Functions are control and management functions not explicitly specified by IEEE 802.11 but essential for large-scale networks: RF monitoring and configuration, WTP firmware loading, network-wide STA state databases, and WTP/AC mutual authentication. These include radio resource measurement, channel assignment, transmit power control, and dynamic channel selection.

Key terminology: WTP (Wireless Termination Point) refers to the physical device with antennas and 802.11 PHY. Access Controller (AC) manages multiple WTPs. The logical Access Point (AP) comprises both 802.11 and CAPWAP functions implemented across one or more physical devices.
sections.eli5: Wi-Fi has two kinds of jobs: ones defined by the Wi-Fi standard (how to send and receive), and ones needed to manage many access points together (where to put them, what to tell them, how secure they are).

sections.title: The Three Architecture Families
sections.content:
Autonomous WLAN Architecture implements all 802.11 and CAPWAP functions in a single WTP device. Each access point is self-contained, configured individually, and monitored via standard protocols like SNMP. This is the traditional approach, with access points sometimes called "fat APs" or "standalone APs". All 16 survey submissions included at least one autonomous implementation reference.

Centralized WLAN Architecture distributes functions between lightweight WTPs and one or more centralized Access Controllers. The AC manages, controls, and configures the WTPs, providing better manageability for large networks. Twelve of the 16 submissions used this approach, split into three variants based on where IEEE 802.11 MAC functions are implemented. Local MAC keeps the entire MAC on the WTP, with the AC handling control and configuration. Split MAC divides MAC functions between WTP (realtime functions like beacon generation) and AC (non-realtime functions like authentication). Remote MAC moves all MAC functions to the AC, leaving the WTP as a PHY-only device.

Distributed WLAN Architecture uses mesh networks where nodes act as both access points for clients and relays for other mesh nodes via 802.11 wireless links. Three submissions used this approach. Mesh nodes can coordinate peer-to-peer without a centralized controller, enabling self-configuration and self-healing. Mesh networks may combine distributed and centralized control where useful.
sections.eli5: Three approaches: one device does everything, a central device tells many devices what to do (with three ways to split the work), or all devices talk to each other like a network.

sections.title: Centralized Architecture Connectivity and Security
sections.content:
WTPs and ACs can be connected through direct connections, layer 2 switches, or layer 3 routers. Local MAC and Split MAC architectures typically support L3 routed connections, while Remote MAC architectures require tighter latency constraints and often use direct or L2 switched connections.

Before exchanging messages, WTPs must discover and authenticate with an AC, download firmware, and establish a control channel. Security considerations differ by variant. In Local MAC, security issues are confined to protecting the control channel and WTP firmware. In Split MAC, encryption keys must sometimes be transferred from the AC to the WTP. In Remote MAC, encryption and decryption occur at the AC, eliminating the need to transfer cryptographic keys.

Centralized architectures generally reduce physical security risks by centralizing secrets in an AC rather than distributing them across WTPs. However, this concentrates all security-sensitive information in one device, making the AC an attractive attack target that requires strict physical and technical controls. The control channel between WTP and AC must be protected against eavesdropping, modification, and replay attacks using encrypted tunnels with integrity and confidentiality protection.
sections.eli5: Access points need to find the controller, prove who they are, get instructions, and talk securely. The controller can be nearby or far away. Putting secrets in one place is safer from theft but riskier if that place is attacked.

sections.title: Architectural Trade-offs and Design Decisions
sections.content:
The three centralized variants represent different trade-offs. Local MAC retains most STA state information on WTPs, providing lower latency and less AC load but less centralized visibility. Remote MAC centralizes all state in the AC, maximizing manageability and simplifying WTP complexity but requiring careful control of AC-to-WTP latency. Split MAC sits in the middle, keeping time-critical functions on WTPs while centralizing policy and authentication at the AC.

Each vendor in the survey made different choices about where to implement each function. Most Local MAC implementations aggregate 802.11 data traffic at the AC for centralized control, though some separate data and control planes by handling data locally. Split MAC implementations consistently implement distribution and integration services at the AC while keeping realtime functions like beacon generation and control frame processing at the WTP. Remote MAC implementations typically use special connectivity like Radio over Fiber (RoF) to minimize latency.

Interoperability is a fundamental market problem. The taxonomy serves as a foundation for defining functional elements as atomic units and standardizing interfaces between elements implemented on different network entities. Future protocol specifications should be developed for any pair of functional elements split across WTPs and ACs.
sections.eli5: Centralizing gives better control but requires fast, reliable connections. Distributed on access points is faster and simpler. Most vendors chose a middle ground where some jobs stay on access points and others go to the controller.
